decision_conditions:
To elaborate on the reason for the London boroguh of Richmonds objection further, we would ask you to note the following commentary from the Conservation/Urban design team:

Due to the height of the proposed blocks, particularly that at 14 storeys, the proposal will be visible from a wide range of views, principally within the Richmond Borough. The ZTV (Zone of Theoretical Visualistaion) within the Heritage Statement illustrates the extent of potential visual impact of the development from within the Borough and neighbouring Boroughs. It is also noted that the site is not located in a tall building zone with the Wandsworth Local Plan and that proposals for tall buildings outside of the designated tall building zones would be resisted as set out in the Wandsworth Local Plan policy LP4. Policy 45 of the Richmond Local Plan takes a similar approach to tall buildings but as the scheme is within Wandsworth, it should be assessed against their respective LP policies. 
Several heritage assets within the Borough will be affected by the proposals through development in their setting. These are set out below: 
•	Barnes Common Conservation Area 
•	White Hart Lane Conservation Area 
•	Thorne Passage Mortlake Conservation Areas 
•	Mortlake Conservation Area 
•	Barnes Green Conservation Area 
•	Queens Road Mortlake Conservation Area 
•	The Terrace Group of Listed buildings and BTMs (incl Barnes Bridge) (as identified in the HS)
•	The Mortlake High Street Group of Listed Buildings and BTMs (as identified in the HS)
•	The Thames Bank group of Listed buildings and BTMs including Chiswick Bridge (as identified in the HS) 
 
An assessment of the significance and impact of these heritage assets and heritage asset groups will be considered in turn below. 

Barnes Common Conservation Area 

The significance of the Barnes Common Conservation Area is defined by and dominated by the 120 acre Common which dominates the south of Barnes and provides a rural setting to the village. The surrounding houses are primarily Victorian or Edwardian, dating from the period between 1850 and 1914 and, of high architectural quality, and relate strongly to the Common.  They are grouped in small clusters of distinctive style and character and are largely well maintained in their original character. Due to the openness of the common area, there are several viewpoints looking out of the conservation area to the surrounding environs. Within the common there is an experience of rural escapism with limited visibility of modern development including tall buildings rising above the tree line. This contributes positively to the character of the conservation area. 

This conservation area is situated just north -east of the application site with one diagonal footpath orientated towards the application site. I note however that a viewpoint has not been produced from this footpath, but I would strongly urge that this is provided. The HS states that views further north largely only give visibility in winter due to the tree cover, but we do not have a view to confirm this, even if wireline. The only view is from Black Poplar Meadow to the north which clearly shows the visibility of the development through the trees and adding the negative appearance of the existing towers on the estate. How it is likely that the view from the path orientated towards the site could be more harmful. The other view provided to show the impact of the development from this CA is view 8 on the periphery of the conservation area. In terms the views provided, it is noted that the towers of the estate are visible and these already detract from the views in terms of negative presence as set out in the Heritage Statement. It is agreed that the towers would likely assume a more dominant aspect which would harmfully affect the experience of the common as an open space with limited visual modern development. Therefore, based on the limited information provided in terms of visuals it is considered that the proposals would have a harmful effect on the character and appearance of the conservation area through development in its setting. This harm would be less than substantial and on the low end of the scale given the presence of towers within the estate already present. 

White Hart Lane Conservation Area 

As set out in the Conservation Area Statement, White Hart Lane conservation area is a small cul de sac development of charming two storey terraced Victorian houses along Eleanor Grove and including a more imposing frontage of three storey commercial buildings to White Hart Lane, forming a gateway to this conservation area. Terraced cottages of painted brick or render enclose Eleanor Grove, either set behind small front gardens and boundaries or opening directly onto the street. A modest pair of later houses terminates the view North along this street. The older properties on the South side have shallow pitched slate roofs behind parapets with moulded cornice and blocking course detail. Younger properties display roofs with projecting eaves supported on corbels. Retained chimneystacks enliven the roofscape here. Houses retain a wealth of detail with moulded window surrounds and either bow windows or square bays with tripartite windows. The larger and well preserved buildings to White Hart Lane are of stock brick with render, set behind well planted front gardens and brick walls to the street. They have canted bay windows, distinctive tripartite windows to the first floor and moulded parapet details, with shallow slate roofs and prominent chimneys behind.

White Hart Lane is an important historic route between the riverside and the Upper Richmond Road. The significance of the Conservation Area is defined by this complex of C19 buildings, with imposing three storey buildings on the street corners and the houses becoming increasingly modest as they are distanced from Eleanor Grove. These White Hart Lane buildings provide a visual gateway into the Grove.

It is noted that despite scoping in the CA, there does not appear to be an assessment of significance or impact on this conservation area. Viewpoint 4 of the Views Analysis is taken from within the conservation area and shows the extent of impact of the development from this point at the junction of Eleanor Grove and White Hart Lane. In this view, the consistent form, height and design of the buildings would be impacted by a dominant tall element which would break the roofline of the buildings. The new development would not directly breach the roofline of the buildings in the conservation area to the east but would distract from the prominence and fine architectural treatment of the building to a much greater extent that the present tall buildings which are visible in some views down White Hart Lane. It is therefore considered that the setting of this conservation area would be harmfully impacted, through the development by virtue of its height and scale and this harm would be at the low end of the less than substantial scale. It is urged that the HS is updated to include an assessment of significance and impact assessment which references view 4.  Please also note that the HS references a list of heritage assets that were agreed with LBRUT officers, but this is not the case. It is likely that this was agreed with Wandsworth. Nonetheless this identifies White Hart Lane CA but then does not produce a full assessment. 

Thorne Passage Mortlake Conservation Area 

The significance of the Thorne Passage Mortlake Conservation Area is defined by the densely developed grid pattern of streets comprising charming and cohesive modest cottages built to a largely consistent scale and form. The cumulative effective the small plots and narrow streets is of a small scale, tightly enclosed environment which is the result of the period of intense development of the area around Barnes in the late 19th century.  As set out in the Conservation Area Statement, Thorne Passage is a particularly unspoilt group of simple cottages with distinctive well planted gardens. The houses of Beverley Path also form a cohesive group, enlivened by red brick stringcourses and door arches, and original canted bay windows.
It is noted that one of the two existing towers on the application site is visible from some views along White Hart Lane although on the opposite side of the road within Mortlake CA. However in viewpoints 4, 6  and 16 the tower will form an incongruous and dominating feature in the street scene, rising above the otherwise consistent roofline of the buildings along White Hart Lane and distracting from the highly cohesive architecture of the buildings. Many of these buildings are also locally listed (BTMs) and their group value and cohesive form will be affected by the presence of the tower above the roofline, drawing the eye away from the buildings and breaking an otherwise largely unaltered and consistent skyline. Accordingly, it is considered that both the Thorne Passage Mortlake CA as well as the BTMs fronting White Hart Lane would be harmfully affected by the development, the harm being less than substantial and at the lower end of the scale. 

Mortlake Conservation Area, Mortlake High St Listed Group and Thames Bank Listed group and BTMs

Mortlake Conservation Area and Thorne Passage Mortlake Conservation Area share boundaries with the two CAs straddling either side of White Hart Lane and part of the Broadway. The Mortlake CA covers a large area, centred on the historic core with St Mary’s Church, surrounded by 18th century listed houses along the riverside and High Street. The conservation area extends to include St Mary’s Churchyard, Vineyard Path, and residential streets such as Alder Road, Fitzgerald Road, and North Worple Way.

The area has a strong relationship with the River Thames and the conservation area encompasses a large stretch of the river and riverbank. The High Street aligns with the historic flood line, while Bull’s Alley and Ship Lane historically provided access to wharfs. Between Chiswick Bridge and Ship Lane, a notable group of mainly 18th century riverside buildings forming the Thames Bank listed group —some with Tudor origins—remains largely intact, with later development respecting their scale and character. Views of this group are particularly important from Chiswick bridge where they read as an important historic composition orientated towards the river. These views not only contribute to the significance of the listed buildings but the conservation area allowing appreciation of the historic relationship of Mortlake to the river. Residential streets such as Fitzgerald Road and Alder Road feature matching two storey brick cottages with characteristic and cohesive architectural details including bay windows, decorative metalwork, slate roofs in diamond patterns, timber porches. The area is also characterised by mature trees, strong landscape quality, and exceptional river views, which feature a harmonious mix of industrial, commercial, and residential uses. 

It is noted that further along the riverside is a small, listed group of buildings which include 115-119 Mortlake High Street and  St Mary Church to the south. It would appear from the visual assessment that these buildings would not be affected by the development. 
Several views from within the conservation area will be affected by the proposed development including the important view from Chiswick Bridge which is a locally protected view and forms a key view to appreciate the listed Thames Bank group (AVR 23). It is noted that the AVRs do not include accumulative views for any of the views. However, in this view, we need to consider the consented Stag Brewery development in the middle ground. The building would form a visible break in the otherwise largely consistent tree line. The current tower at Lennox forms a modest break in the skyline however the proposed tower would form a more prominent feature rising above the tree line and affecting the character and spatial qualities of this view and its contribution to the appearance of the conservation area. 

Another view is AVR 16 which affects several conservation areas as they converge at this point along White Hart Lane. As set out in the HS, the addition of the tower above the roofline would be disruptive of the cohesive historic streetscape. This will result in less than substantial harm to the appearance of the conservation area. When considering all the views and the importance of such views on the significance of the conservation area as a whole, a medium level of less than substantial harm would result from the proposals. In terms of the Thames Bank listed building group, a modest level of harm would result from impacts on the view from Chiswick Bridge although this needs to be reviewed once a cumulative AVR is produced. 

Barnes Green Conservation Area and the Terrace listed group and BTMS

The Barnes Green Conservation Area covers the historic core of Barnes as well as late 19th century and early 20th century residential development to the east and west. The river and the Green are key defining features of the area, with the latter acting as the focus for the village.  The area is forms of several character areas, the historic core sub-area contains the major part of the early development of Barnes, with buildings ranging in date from the 17th to 21st centuries, with this architectural variety making a strong contribution to the overall significance of the area.  The Malthouse Passage/Stanton Road sub-area represents small residential enclaves with a distinct character, tucked away from the busy main streets of Barnes. The Victorian and Edwardian Residential character area comprises the bulk of the built environment of the Conservation Area outside of the historic core and are reflective of the extensive development undertaken in Barnes in the last decades of the 19th century and into the 20th century. The Lion Houses, built between 1899 and 1903 are the most distinctive of this development

Barnes has retained some of its rural village character into the 19th century, only undergoing transformation in the late 19th and early 20th centuries from a rural settlement into a suburban area, reflecting the urban sprawl of London in this period. Whilst Barnes has been encroached on by this suburban development, its rural character remains clearly legible in the form of the Green and its framing architecture which contributes to its significance. The river also forms a key element of its significance forming a key contributor to the layout and development of the area.
It is noted that the HS states that there is an impact on Barnes Green CA (para 5.12) in their impact assessment but then does not undertake a full assessment. Only Barnes Common CA, Priory Hospital LB and Thorne Passage and Mortlake CAs are fully assessed. However, several views are affected by the development both within the Barnes Green conservation area and looking towards it from the north side of the bank at Dukes Meadow. These include views 12,19  20 and 21. View 24 also affects the part of the setting of the CA but it is noted that the development would not be visible from this point sitting lower that n the development along the river. In view 19, 20 the development will be visible in a gap in the building line which fronts the riverside. The buildings in this view form a fine quality historic composition many of which are listed and form part of the ‘terrace listed group’. The development, whilst situated in the background would, nonetheless form an incongruent feature in the view, notably the tower. It would also fill the visual gap between the mansion blocks to the left and no 26 The Terrace (BTM) to the right in the view. In view 12, which is a rendered view, the building would be even more visually prominent, breaking the important and consistent historic roofline of the buildings along The Terrace, which include listed buildings and BTMs. The building would therefore cause less than substantial harm to both the appearance of the CA and the setting of this historic group of buildings, rising above the roofline and forming an incongruous and out of place feature that would draw the eye away from the buildings and their architectural composition. 
 In view 21, whilst this is a distance view and other taller buildings are featured, namely the towers of Lennox as existing, the addition of the proposed tower would rise above the otherwise consistent roofline of the buildings which forms a positive feature of the view and the conservation area.  

Overall, the proposed tower element of the development would cause less than substantial harm to the character and appearance of the conservation area, featuring in several important views within and towards the CA. As noted above, the tower would also cause less than substantial harm to the setting of the terraced group of listed and locally listed buildings. 

Queens Road Mortlake Conservation Area 

The conservation area is characterised by modest two-storey Victorian cottages along narrow streets, with the earliest properties found along Queens Road. This architectural character and spatial layout contribute greatly to the areas significance, which is also defined by Mortlake Cemetery which forms the eastern part of the Conservation Area. This is a good example of a Victorian cemetery with some fine mature trees. The adjoining terraces of small Victorian cottages, some of which face onto narrow alleyways and have unusual embellishments, possess a charming sense of space. This area forms one of the earliest settlements in Mortlake, evidenced by the historic street pattern.

One view has been provided from this conservation area, view 14 and it is taken from within the cemetery which forms the central feature of the CA. It is not clear in the view if the development would be sited in front of behind the existing tower, but it would rise above the existing tower and form a more prominent feature in the view. It is noted that the sky line of the cemetery already features taller element and the building remains below the tree line so in the summer months, it would largely be obscured, thus reducing the harm, but in the winter months it would form a visual and incongruous feature, being much taller than the existing buildings and thus interrupting one’s appreciation of the openness and architecture of this space. A negligible amount of less than substantial harm would therefore be caused to this conservation area. 

Other heritage assets 

It is noted from the visuals, that the Richmond CA and RPAG will not be affected by the development nor the strategic protected view from Sawyer’s Hill and therefore no harm has been identified to result from the development.
description: 2025/4170 - Construction of 81 new affordable units (use class C3) across two buildings ranging from 6 to 14 storeys, incorporating ground floor community floorspace (use class E(d) and F2). Demolition of existing buildings, MUGA and structures and stopping up of part of Arabella Drive, provision of new and replacement open space and play space, landscape and public realm improvements including reorganistation of car parking and carriageway on Lodovick Walk. Removal and replacement of existing pedestrian and stepped access to existing homes at 11-15 Ludovick Walk and other associated work.
